topic: How do trains stay on the tracks?

claims.claim: A pair of train wheels is fixed rigidly to one solid axle (a wheelset), so both wheels turn at the same rate.
Train wheel treads are slightly conical (tapered): larger in diameter next to the flange and narrowing towards the outside.
claims.note: S1 gives a 1:20 taper example; the video uses no numbers

claims.claim: A wheelset with conical treads tends to centre itself between the rails; the coned tread, not the flange, is the main way a moving train stays aligned.
claims.note: sources state self-centring but do not detail the straight-track mechanism step by step; the video shows only the drift and the return to centre

claims.claim: On a curve the wheelset shifts towards the outer rail; the outer wheel rolls on a larger diameter and covers more distance per turn, the inner wheel on a smaller one, so the solid axle follows the curve without the slipping cylindrical wheels would suffer.
claims.note: 'without slipping' is stated by S1; S2 calls it self-steering

claims.claim: Flanges are lips on the inner side of each wheel; they act when strong sideways forces push the wheelset beyond its normal range, for example at speed on a bend, in strong crosswinds or over track defects.

guardrails: no numbers for weight, speed, taper or diameters (none are needed and weight/speed were not sourced)
the taper is exaggerated in the art for visibility; it is described as slight
do not say flanges never touch the rail; say they are the backup for strong sideways pushes
do not mention cant/superelevation or hunting oscillation (not covered by both sources)
trains, rails and people are illustrative, not a specific railway
